topic: Mastering Wordle: Information Theory and Optimal Strategies
target_audience: University students interested in Computer Science and Data Analytics

sections.title: The Core Concept: Entropy
sections.content: Introduce information entropy (Shannon Entropy) as the measure of uncertainty reduction. Explain that each guess is a tool to eliminate the maximum number of impossible candidates from the dictionary.
sections.example: Imagine a bowl of 2,300 M&Ms (the dictionary). A good guess is like a sieve that removes as many as possible, leaving only a small, manageable handful.

sections.title: Prerequisite: Probability & Visual Mapping
sections.content: Briefly define the 'State Space' of a guess (Green, Yellow, Gray). Visualize the game as a Decision Tree where every branch reduces the branching factor of the search space.
sections.example: Visualizing the search space as a Venn Diagram where the intersection of 'contains A' and 'ends in E' shrinks the potential word pool from 2,300 to 50.

sections.title: Algorithmic Strategy: The 'Best' First Guess
sections.content: Analyze why high-frequency letters (e.g., E, A, R, I, O, T) are superior. Introduce the algorithm: Minimax (minimizing the maximum remaining words) or Max Entropy.
sections.example: Comparing 'XYLYL' (low entropy) vs 'CRANE' (high entropy). Show a bar chart animation where 'CRANE' leaves a more uniform distribution of potential remaining sets.

sections.title: Tactical Application: The 'Hard Mode' Trap
sections.content: Discuss the trade-off between choosing the 'most likely' word versus the 'best information' word. Sometimes, sacrificing a guess to eliminate multiple letter options is statistically better.
sections.example: A clever 'Robot Assistant' character choosing 'SLATE' to eliminate 5 common letters, even though it knows 'SLATE' isn't the target, to guarantee the answer on turn 3.

sections.title: Summary and Synthesis
sections.content: Recap: Information Theory transforms Wordle from a game of intuition into a game of computational efficiency. The optimal path is always minimizing the 'bits' of remaining uncertainty.
sections.example: A quick visual animation: Starting with a giant cloud of 2,300 words, seeing it collapse into a single point after just 3 optimized moves.
